A 67-year-old man with a history of mood disorder, Parkinson's disease, hyperlipidemia, and mild cognitive impairment presented after an unwitnessed fall at home. Family noticed increasing weakness, fatigue, and confusion a few weeks before presentation. Patient reported decreased appetite and mild dyspnea, especially on exertion. No significant weight loss, dysphagia, or odynophagia. No history of smoking.
Patient was in no acute distress. Neurologic examination revealed resting tremors in bilateral hands but was otherwise nonfocal. Abdominal examination was unremarkable.

A 71-year-old man presented with three weeks of jaundice, weight loss, abdominal pain, and dark-colored urine. He also reported bilateral lower-extremity weakness that was most noticeable when attempting to arise from a chair, resulting in several ground-level falls. He had no history of autoimmune or neuromuscular conditions. Despite his recent falls, he did not have any prolonged periods of being down that could contribute to muscle injury. He had been taking atorvastatin as a home medication.
Physical findings included:- Jaundice and significant scleral icterus- Epigastric tenderness without guarding or rebound- Mild weakness in bilateral hip flexor muscles

A 29-year-old woman from the Dominican Republic, who moved to the United States in 2014, presented in January 2016 for prenatal care. A purified protein derivative skin test was positive (21 mm). In January 2022, she was started on rifampin (300 mg daily) for a planned 4-month course. She was taking no other medications. After three months of therapy, she experienced two days of nausea, vomiting, and subjective fevers.
Initial presentation showed no significant physical examination findings noted in the case report.
